The test image shows a longitudinal cross-section of a soybean stem held open, revealing brown/orange discoloration of the internal pith tissue, while the outer stem remains green. Key candidates: **Brown Stem Rot** (brown pith) vs **Sudden Death Syndrome** (white pith).

The Brown Stem Rot reference shows stems with the pith visible — the bottom-right panel shows a split stem. The SDS reference shows interveinal chlorosis on leaves and root damage. 

The test image's brown/orange pith with green outer stem is the hallmark of Brown Stem Rot. Let me view a few more references to confirm and rule out Fusarium/Phytophthora:

I've now viewed 12 reference images. Here's my analysis:

**Test image observations:**
- Soybean stem held open (longitudinal cross-section)
- **Outer stem is green** — plant still living/growing
- **Pith shows clear brown/orange-brown discoloration** throughout the interior
- Stem surface has normal soybean pubescence (hairs)

**Key differential:**
| Disease | Pith color | Match? |
|---|---|---|
| Brown Stem Rot | **Brown** (diagnostic) | ✅ Perfect match |
| Sudden Death Syndrome | White/cream (pith stays white) | ❌ |
| Charcoal Rot | Very dark/black (charcoal-like) with microsclerotia | ❌ |
| Fusarium | Reddish-brown vascular discoloration, root-focused | ❌ |
| Phytophthora | Dark chocolate-brown external stem lesion, not pith | ❌ |

The brown/orange pith discoloration visible in the split green stem is the **classic and diagnostic feature of Brown Stem Rot** — the knowledge base even notes "the pith remains brown unlike in sudden death syndrome where it stays white or cream-colored," confirming this distinction is the key differentiator.
